title: Trent on grace
hookLine: justification begins with grace, received in faith, and bears fruit in works

lines: JAMES: FAITH WITHOUT WORKS IS DEAD.
cards: Two lines, one Bible. Paul writes to the Ephesians, in the Douay-Rheims, "For by grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, for it is the gift of God." James writes, "faith without works is dead."

Read either one alone and it can sound like the whole story. The reformers leaned hard on Paul, and some of them were uneasy with James. At Trent, the bishops spent a long time trying to hold both lines in one hand.

teach.b: The council's decree on justification, being made right with God, moves in a careful order. First, grace begins it.
The beginning, it says, comes from God's grace, which goes ahead of us and calls us without any merit of our own. We don't start the journey; God does.
Second, faith receives it. The decree calls faith the beginning of human salvation, the foundation and root of all justification.
And it adds a striking line: nothing that comes before justification, neither faith nor works, earns the grace of justification. It's a gift.
Third, it bears fruit. For Trent, justification isn't only having sins forgiven; it's being made new on the inside.

teach.h: NO ONE EARNS IT BY WORKS.
teach.b: A person made new grows, and that growth shows in love and in works.
That's where James comes in: works aren't the price of grace. They're what grace does when it's alive in someone. Then, the guardrail.

Among its canons, the council condemned the idea that a person can be made right with God by their own works, without God's grace through Christ. Some people imagine Catholics believe you earn your way to God.
Trent rules that out: good works matter, but they grow from grace, never apart from it. Catholics and Lutherans still differ on how this works in a person.
But the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation have since signed a joint declaration saying they share a basic understanding of justification by grace.

how: Catholics are taught that justification begins with God's grace, given in baptism, received in faith and growing through love and good works; the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation have signed a joint declaration on the doctrine of justification.

o: sins forgiven in confession, and nothing more
being made right with God, beginning with grace
earning God's favor through enough good works

games.q: Trent on grace — tap the pairs.
p: goes ahead and calls us first

s: Trent taught that Catholics earn heaven by their works
it condemned the idea of being made right with God by works without grace.
Trent said nothing before justification, faith or works, earns it
the decree calls it a gift; faith is the root, not a payment.
Catholics and Lutherans have never agreed on anything about justification
they have since signed a joint declaration on a basic shared understanding.

games.q: you're drafting Trent's decree. one side quotes Paul on grace; another quotes James on works. what do you write?
o: works first, then grace as a reward.
grace first, received in faith, bearing fruit in works.
faith alone, and works don't matter.
games.why: the decree begins with grace that calls us without merit, roots it in faith, and sees works as grace's fruit.

practice: Bring to mind three good things in your life you didn't earn: a meal someone else cooked, someone who loved you before you'd done anything, a morning you were given.
Let each one sit for a few breaths and just receive it, without turning it into a to-do list. If you pray, say thank you, simply, once for each; if you don't, just notice them.

carryVoice: Your line: grace first. The gift comes before any good we do. Day seven hundred eighty-six, done.
